rationale: A wins because it treats the ugliest fact as the story and the gate: "If the company will not disclose the source, do not pitch this angle." That is adult supervision. B has real shapes, but it keeps overreaching with lines like "Patients priced out of branded weight-loss drugs" and "branded drugmakers want it stopped" when the fact block only gives cheaper access and manufacturer pushback.
gaps_in_A: "Hims & Hers won't say where its compounded semaglutide comes from" overstates the record. The update says the supply source is not named, not that the company refused to say.
"a prescription by video" invents the modality. The fact block says telehealth visit, not video.

"ongoing FDA-versus-compounders dispute that is already being reported" imports an outside news context the set was not given. The FDA warning and manufacturer pushback are enough; don't decorate them.
gaps_in_B: "branded drugmakers want it stopped" is too strong. The facts say branded manufacturers have pushed back, not that they are seeking to stop this specific launch.
"Hims & Hers is scaling them anyway" turns a launch into scale. That may be true later; it is not in the update.
"Patients priced out of branded weight-loss drugs" invents the patient condition. No patient, price point, or affordability data beyond "a fraction" appears in the facts.

It notices "currently unnamed — a hole, not a detail" but buries the supply-source problem inside proof instead of making it a standalone supply-chain/regulatory story. That is the sharpest reporter question in the whole update.
